code.title: Same-origin check: scheme, host and port

followUps: Same-site is looser: it compares only the registrable domain (like example.com), ignoring subdomains and ports, while same-origin needs scheme, host and port all equal. So app.example.com and api.example.com are cross-origin but same-site. Cookies and SameSite rules use same-site; script access (fetch reads, DOM, storage) uses same-origin. Browsers also treat a scheme change (http vs https) as cross-site in the modern "schemeful" definition.

Use window.postMessage. The sender calls target.postMessage(data, "https://b.com") with an exact target origin, never "*" for private data. The receiver listens for message events and checks event.origin against an allowlist before trusting event.data. Other legitimate routes are CORS for fetch, and BroadcastChannel or MessageChannel between same-origin contexts. Setting document.domain is deprecated and should be avoided.

An opaque origin is an origin with no usable scheme, host or port, serialised as the string "null", and it is never equal to any other origin, even another opaque one. It is given to sandboxed iframes (without allow-same-origin), data: URLs, local file: pages in many browsers, and some redirects. Such pages cannot read normal storage or cookies, and requests from them send Origin: null, which is why servers must never allowlist null.

code.title: Does this request trigger a CORS preflight?

followUps: A form POST can already be sent cross-origin by a plain HTML page, so allowing it adds no new power for attackers; the browser skips the preflight. A JSON body needs Content-Type: application/json, which HTML forms cannot produce, so it is a new capability that old servers never expected. The preflight asks the server for permission first. Example: text/plain POST is simple, application/json POST is not, even with the same bytes.

Cache it and send fewer of them. Set Access-Control-Max-Age (for example 600 seconds; Chrome caps it at 7200 and Firefox at 86400), so repeat calls reuse the answer. Avoid custom headers and JSON content type where a simple request will do, and serve the API on the same origin through a proxy so no CORS is needed at all. Each preflight costs one extra round trip, such as 80 ms on a mobile link, so 10 distinct URLs can add 800 ms if nothing is cached. Note the cache is keyed per URL, origin and headers.

Because the preflight is sent without credentials, so an auth middleware that demands a cookie or Authorization header rejects it. The browser never attaches those to OPTIONS. Fix it by answering OPTIONS before authentication runs, returning 204 with the Access-Control-Allow-* headers, and only checking auth on the real request. Also check that a redirect (say http to https or a missing trailing slash) is not answering OPTIONS, because preflights must not be redirected.

Then the browser may keep serving a cached response made for a different origin, so a user on one site sees headers meant for another, or no headers at all. Fix it by sending Vary: Origin whenever the allowed origin depends on the request, so the CDN stores one copy per origin. Also make sure the CDN forwards the Origin header to the origin server and does not strip or cache OPTIONS responses wrongly. A purge may be needed after the fix.

In dev, run a proxy (for example the dev server forwarding /api to localhost:8080) so the browser sees one origin and no CORS is involved, or allow http://localhost:3000 explicitly. In prod, use an exact allowlist such as https://app.example.com read from config, plus Vary: Origin. Do not ship a dev wildcard to production, and keep the same code path in both so tests catch mistakes. Preferably serve UI and API under one domain behind a gateway.

Pick Strict when the app has no need to arrive logged in from outside links, such as banking, admin consoles or a payment confirmation. With Strict the cookie is not sent on any cross-site request, even clicking a link from email, so the user lands as logged out and sees the login page once. Lax keeps that first navigation logged in. A common design is Lax for the main session and a Strict cookie for sensitive actions.

When the cookie must travel on cross-site requests: an embedded widget or iframe that keeps a login, a payment or chat widget used on partner sites, or a cross-site fetch with credentials to your API. The cookie then needs SameSite=None; Secure, which also means HTTPS only. Because it is sent from any site, it brings back CSRF risk, so you must add CSRF tokens and check Origin. Browsers also reject None without Secure, and some may block it as third-party.

A third-party cookie is one set or sent by a domain different from the page the user is on, used for ads, tracking and embedded logins. Safari and Firefox block them by default, and Chrome has moved toward user-controlled choice rather than a full removal. Plan as if they will not work: use first-party cookies, same-site subdomains, token exchange or the Storage Access API, and for tracking-free embeds consider partitioned cookies (Partitioned attribute, CHIPS), which are keyed per top-level site.

code.title: Escaping untrusted text before rendering as HTML

followUps: Because the right encoding depends on where the data lands, and that is only known at output time. Escaping on input stores one mangled version: O'Brien in a database looks wrong in JSON, CSV or a mobile app, and it is easy to double-encode. HTML needs <, an attribute needs quotes escaped, a URL needs percent-encoding, JS strings need other rules. So store raw data (after validation) and encode for the specific context each time you render it.

Mostly, but not fully. React escapes text in JSX, so {userInput} is safe. The holes are dangerouslySetInnerHTML, href or src values like javascript:alert(1), server-side rendering of unescaped strings, vulnerable third-party libraries, and DOM code outside React (ref.innerHTML). Treat every one of those as a sink: validate URL schemes to http/https, sanitize any HTML with DOMPurify, and lint against raw HTML use.

Mutation XSS (mXSS) happens when sanitized HTML is safe as a string, but the browser parser rewrites it when inserting into the DOM, and the rewritten form contains a script or handler. Odd nesting such as <svg><style> or <noscript> can flip meaning between parses. Defences: use a maintained sanitizer (DOMPurify) and keep it updated, sanitize in the same parser context you render in, avoid re-serialising and re-inserting sanitized output, and add Trusted Types and CSP as backstops.

Rotation means every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If a thief copies a token and uses it, then the real user tries the old token (or the reverse), the server sees an already-used token. It cannot tell who is honest, so it revokes the whole token family and forces a new login. Example: token R1 is used to get R2; if R1 shows up again, the server kills R2 and everything after it. This limits theft to one refresh window.

Native apps have no same-origin browser model and no XSS on a web page, so tokens can sit in the OS secure store (Keychain on iOS, Keystore on Android) instead of localStorage. Use the authorization code flow with PKCE through the system browser, not an embedded web view, and use a custom or claimed HTTPS redirect URI. Bind tokens to the device where possible. Main new risks are a rooted device, a stolen backup and other apps intercepting redirects.

The implicit flow returned the access token directly in the URL fragment, where it leaks through browser history, referrer headers, logs and malicious scripts, and it could not use refresh tokens or client authentication. Token injection attacks were also hard to stop. The current advice (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP, OAuth 2.1) is the authorization code flow with PKCE for SPAs too: the app gets a one-time code, then exchanges it with a secret code verifier. Tokens never appear in the URL.

code.title: CSRF synchronizer token check

followUps: A CSRF token does not stop XSS because injected script runs inside your page, so it can read the token from the DOM or from a same-origin fetch and send it with the forged request. The token only proves the request came from a page that could read your HTML, and an XSS attacker is exactly that. That is why CSRF defence assumes XSS is separately prevented. In other words, any XSS defeats CSRF protection, so fix XSS first.

Yes, if auth is by cookies. A browser can send a cross-site fetch with credentials: "include", and some servers accept a text/plain body that happens to parse as JSON, so JSON alone does not protect you. It is safe only if the API strictly requires Content-Type: application/json (which forces a preflight that CORS rejects) or a custom header, and uses SameSite cookies. If auth is a bearer token in an Authorization header, CSRF is not a concern, because browsers do not attach it automatically.

In login CSRF the attacker forges a login request that signs the victim into the attacker's account. The victim then unknowingly saves data (search history, cards, documents) into an account the attacker controls and later reads. The defence is the same as normal CSRF: a token on the login form (even before a session exists, via a pre-session cookie), SameSite cookies and Origin checks. Also rotate the session id on login.

A host allowlist like script-src cdn.example.com allows every script on that host, including old libraries, JSONP endpoints or user uploads, any of which an attacker can use to run code, and Google research found most allowlists were bypassable. A nonce is a random value per response, so only tags carrying that exact value run, and the attacker cannot guess a fresh 128-bit value. With strict-dynamic, trusted scripts can load others without listing hosts. Nonces must be unpredictable and never reused across responses.

Third-party tags (analytics, ad networks, chat, tag managers) often inject inline scripts, load more scripts from unknown hosts, use eval or write styles inline, so a strict policy blocks them. Options: give them nonces and rely on strict-dynamic, replace the vendor snippet with a self-hosted copy plus SRI, move them to a sandboxed iframe, drop the ones without business value, and watch the Report-Only reports to see what actually loads. Each exemption weakens the policy, so keep a list with owners.

Trusted Types is a browser feature, switched on with the CSP directive require-trusted-types-for 'script', that makes dangerous DOM sinks such as innerHTML, eval and script.src accept only special typed objects, not plain strings. Code must pass data through a named policy (for example one that runs DOMPurify), so there are only a few audited places that can create HTML. This stops most DOM-based XSS by design, and violations can be reported before enforcing.

Because the attacker can run script in their own page and move that frame, and several tricks defeat such code: a sandboxed iframe (sandbox without allow-top-navigation) disables the frame-buster, the onbeforeunload handler can cancel its redirect, and older browsers can be tricked in other ways. A client-side check also runs only after the page loads. A response header like frame-ancestors is enforced by the browser before rendering, so the attacker cannot turn it off.

List the partner's exact origin in CSP: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.example.com. The browser then allows framing from your own site and that one partner, and blocks everyone else. Skip X-Frame-Options there, because its ALLOW-FROM form is obsolete and ignored by modern browsers (browsers that support both follow CSP). If partners vary, choose the header per request from a server-side allowlist, and tell them to use HTTPS. For extra safety, ask the user to confirm sensitive actions even when embedded.

Through the Alt-Svc response header, or an HTTPS/SVCB DNS record. The browser first connects over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 (TCP) and reads something like Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400, which says "HTTP/3 is available on UDP port 443 for a day". On the next request it tries QUIC, and quietly falls back to TCP if UDP is blocked by a firewall. DNS HTTPS records let it try HTTP/3 even on the first visit.

0-RTT lets a returning client send data in its first packet, saving a round trip, but that data can be replayed by an attacker who captured it, so the server may process it twice. For a read-only GET this is harmless; for "transfer 100" it is not. Servers should accept 0-RTT only for idempotent requests, or reject it, and use anti-replay protection or single-use tickets. Frontend code should not rely on it for state-changing calls without idempotency keys.

Less than before, but yes. With HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, 100 tiny files no longer cost 100 connections, so you do not need one giant bundle. Still, hundreds of requests add header and scheduling cost, lose compression across files and delay discovery of imports. The usual balance is a few dozen route-based chunks with long-cache hashed names: shared vendor chunk, per-page chunk, and preload for critical ones. Measure with real network throttling; a 1 MB bundle that is mostly unused is worse than five 100 KB chunks you actually need.

It is a list of domains built into browsers that are always loaded over HTTPS, even on the very first visit, which plain HSTS cannot cover (the first request is still http). To join, serve HSTS with max-age of at least one year, includeSubDomains and preload, redirect http to https, then submit the domain. Removal takes months of browser releases, so every subdomain must support HTTPS permanently before you submit; one internal http-only subdomain will break.

The CDN or server must serve the file with CORS headers when the page loads it from another origin: the tag needs crossorigin="anonymous" and the response must include Access-Control-Allow-Origin, otherwise the browser cannot check the hash and blocks the script. The bytes must also be exactly what you hashed, so no on-the-fly minification, or rewriting of the file by the CDN, and pinned versions rather than "latest". When the library updates, regenerate the sha384-... value.

code.title: CORS: reflected origin vs strict allowlist

followUps: The origin null is sent by sandboxed iframes, data: URLs and local files, and an attacker can create one easily from any page by using <iframe sandbox srcdoc=...>. If your server answers Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null with credentials, the attacker's sandboxed frame can read your API with the victim's cookies. Since null cannot identify one trustworthy site, never put it on an allowlist, not even for local testing in production.

The risk is much smaller, because browsers do not attach a bearer token automatically; the attacker's page does not have it, so a reflected origin leaks nothing without it. Still avoid reflecting everything: it exposes any endpoint that trusts the network location (internal IPs, intranet, localhost services), and a later change to cookies would silently become dangerous. Without credentials a plain Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is acceptable for genuinely public data. Never combine * with credentials; browsers reject it.

For an internal tool, I would drop the heavy parts that mainly fight an open internet: preload and strict third-party isolation, device binding, step-up auth for every action, and the full BFF if SSO already protects it behind a VPN or identity-aware proxy. I would keep the basics: HTTPS and HSTS, SSO with short sessions, SameSite cookies, CSRF checks, escaped output, a decent CSP, and frame-ancestors. Internal does not mean trusted, because a compromised laptop or a phishing link still reaches it.

Turn each control into an automated test or monitor. A CI test fetches key pages and asserts the exact headers (CSP, HSTS, cookie flags, frame-ancestors). A browser test (Playwright) sends a hostile Origin and verifies no CORS headers come back. Report-Only and enforced CSP reports feed an alert if violations spike. Add scanners (ZAP, header checkers) on a schedule, dependency audits in the pipeline, and a regular penetration test. Fail the build when a header disappears, as a CDN or proxy change can remove it silently.

Passkeys (WebAuthn) replace passwords with a per-site key pair, so there is nothing to phish or reuse, and the browser only signs for the real origin. That removes password reset and credential-stuffing paths, but the session after login still needs all the cookie, CSRF and XSS controls above. Design points: offer passkeys as the primary method with a secure recovery path (recovery is often the weakest link), support multiple devices, require user verification for transfers, and still use step-up auth for high-risk actions.
